content: Access to information, whether online or offline, should be supported by regularly updated resources such as the WHO Hinari e-Granary system and open-source journals. A culture of evidence-based practice can be fostered by sharing case studies and developing treatment protocols within prosthetics and orthotics teams. Mentorship programs, either in person or through e-health platforms, can pair mentors with personnel to analyze case studies, helping to embed new skills and knowledge after short courses. For instance, a mentor may supervise a series of prosthetics and orthotics treatments until the recipient is confident in applying new techniques. Prosthetics and orthotics personnel should remain committed to continuous professional development (CPD) and reflective practice. A mandatory amount of CPD per year should be a condition of employment. Experienced personnel should engage in annual professional development planning, identifying their CPD needs in collaboration with employers and professional associations to create and implement individual development plans. Training courses in prosthetics and orthotics provide foundational knowledge for practice, but no graduate will master all fields immediately. Expertise is developed through daily practice, collaboration with colleagues and mentors, and participation in courses and seminars as part of CPD. Roles within prosthetics and orthotics evolve over time to meet service needs and complement the skills of other rehabilitation team members. In larger units, personnel may specialize in narrower areas, such as upper-limb prosthetics, diabetic footwear, or sports injuries, enhancing proficiency and service quality while reducing the need for extensive cross-training. This involves assessing service needs, calculating personnel requirements, profiling the existing workforce, and addressing gaps between current supply and future demand. Workforce development plans should align with national population census cycles and consider the contributions of other disciplines, such as physicians and rehabilitation professionals, to prosthetics and orthotics services. Retention of personnel is critical, as training and mentoring represent significant financial investments. Strategies to motivate professionals include equitable recognition of the profession, career opportunities, competitive salaries, supportive working environments, and the ability to influence workplace decisions. Migration of professionals from lowto high-income countries or rural to urban areas is a challenge, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Professional regulation is necessary to protect users from harm. Prosthetics and orthotics clinicians should be regulated by an independent state body that maintains a register of practicing professionals. Technicians and other technical personnel should work under the supervision of certified clinicians who assume responsibility for their conduct. Professional recognition is vital for motivation, retention, and development. Awareness of the distinct roles and titles of prosthetists, orthotists, associates, and technicians should be raised, and their employment conditions should align with those of other healthcare professionals. Professional associations and societies can further the development of the field by promoting evidence-based practice, sharing best practices, and engaging with regulators and national planners. User-centered prosthetics and orthotics services should prioritize accessibility, respect, safety, and informed decision-making. Users should have the right to choose their service provider and technology, fostering competition and improving service quality. Accessible services must be financially, physically, and geographically equitable, ensuring that all individuals in need can receive appropriate care.
